speaker: ALEX
text: Welcome back. This episode is a companion to the glossary, so the goal is simple: make GitHub words feel less mysterious when you hear them in a workshop, an issue, or a pull request.

speaker: JAMIE
text: I love a glossary episode because half the stress of open source is hearing a familiar word used in a very specific way. Like, I know what a branch is in a tree. Git has other plans.

speaker: ALEX
text: Exactly. The glossary is there for quick lookup across the whole workshop. Terms are grouped by topic, and there is also an alphabetical quick reference near the end when you already know the word you need.

speaker: JAMIE
text: And the navigation tips matter. If you use a screen reader, headings are your friend here. Jump by headings, open the elements list, and type a few letters of the term.

speaker: ALEX
text: If you use magnification, the term headings and the alphabetical table are useful because each row stands on its own. And anyone can use Control-F in the browser to search directly for a word like remote, stash, or ARIA.

speaker: JAMIE
text: Let's also say pronunciations as we go, because some of these terms are awkward when you only read them.

speaker: ALEX
text: Yes. Git is pronounced with a hard G, like get with an i sound. Repo is REE-poh, short for repository. Org is just org, short for organization. And PR is usually spoken as the letters P R, meaning pull request.

speaker: JAMIE
text: Good. My shoulders just dropped a little.

speaker: ALEX
text: A repository, often shortened to repo, is the project container. It holds the files, folders, documentation, and the full history of changes.

speaker: JAMIE
text: So it is more than a folder. It is a folder with memory.

speaker: ALEX
text: Right. A repository on GitHub has an address like github.com, then the owner name, then the repo name. If the owner is a group account, that group is called an organization, or org.

speaker: JAMIE
text: So in microsoft slash vscode, microsoft is the organization and vscode is the repository.

speaker: ALEX
text: Exactly. A fork is your personal copy of someone else's repository on GitHub. You use a fork when you do not have permission to write directly to the original project, but you still want to propose changes.

speaker: JAMIE
text: And clone is different from fork, right? That pair always trips people up.

speaker: ALEX
text: Fork means a copy under your GitHub account. Clone means a copy on your computer, where you can work in VS Code or another editor. A common workflow is fork the project on GitHub, then clone your fork to your computer.

speaker: JAMIE
text: Where do remotes fit into that?

speaker: ALEX
text: A remote is a named connection from your local Git repository to a repository hosted somewhere else, usually GitHub. The remote named origin usually points to the repo you cloned from. If you cloned your fork, origin points to your fork.

speaker: JAMIE
text: And upstream is the original project you forked from.

speaker: ALEX
text: Yes. You can see remotes with `git remote -v`. You can add the original project as upstream with a command like `git remote add upstream https://github.com/original-owner/repo.git`.

speaker: JAMIE
text: So local means on my computer, remote means hosted elsewhere, origin is usually my GitHub copy, and upstream is the original project.

speaker: ALEX
text: That is the usual setup. You may also hear downstream, which means something based on another project. A fork is downstream from the original because it receives changes from that original source.

speaker: JAMIE
text: Before we leave the project container words, what is dot gitignore?

speaker: ALEX
text: `.gitignore` is a special file that tells Git not to track certain files. You use it for temporary operating system files, build outputs like `dist/` or `build/`, dependency folders like `node_modules/`, editor folders like `.vscode/`, and secret files like `.env`.

speaker: JAMIE
text: Important warning there: dot gitignore does not magically erase something that was already committed.

speaker: ALEX
text: Correct. It only ignores untracked files. If a file is already tracked by Git, you remove it from tracking with `git rm --cached filename`, then add the pattern to `.gitignore`, then commit that change.

speaker: ALEX
text: A branch is a separate line of development inside a repository. The main branch, usually called `main`, is often the stable version of the project.

speaker: JAMIE
text: And sometimes older projects use `master`, so if I hear that, it is also a branch name, not a different tool.

speaker: ALEX
text: Right. Common branch names include `main`, sometimes `develop`, and then names like `feature/add-search`, `fix/broken-button`, or `docs/update-readme`. The name should help people understand the purpose of the work.

speaker: JAMIE
text: Then a commit is the saved checkpoint.

speaker: ALEX
text: Yes. A commit records a snapshot of changes, a message, the author, a timestamp, and a unique identifier called a SHA hash. SHA is often pronounced shah, though spelling S H A is also common.

speaker: JAMIE
text: Commit messages have a style too, don't they?

speaker: ALEX
text: They do. A good message says what the change does, often in the imperative mood: `Fix typo in README`, not `Fixed typo` or `Fixing typo`. Longer commit messages can include a short title, a blank line, and then a body explaining why the change was made.

speaker: JAMIE
text: And a diff is how we inspect the change.

speaker: ALEX
text: A diff, short for difference, shows what changed between two versions. Added lines are usually shown with a plus sign, removed lines with a minus sign, and unchanged lines appear as context.

speaker: JAMIE
text: That is what I am reading on the Files Changed tab of a pull request.

speaker: ALEX
text: Exactly. Push, pull, and fetch are the movement words. Push sends your local commits up to a remote. Fetch downloads remote changes so you can inspect them. Pull fetches changes and then integrates them into your current branch.

speaker: JAMIE
text: So fetch is the cautious look, and pull is the update that changes my branch.

speaker: ALEX
text: An issue is a discussion item in a GitHub repository. People use issues to report bugs, request features, ask questions, discuss ideas, and track work.

speaker: JAMIE
text: Issues also have numbers, like number 42, and they can have labels, assignees, milestones, and comments.

speaker: ALEX
text: Yes. A pull request, or PR, is a proposal to merge changes from one branch into another. It includes the branch information, the diff, a description of what changed and why, and a place for discussion.

speaker: JAMIE
text: The name still sounds a little odd. It means I am asking maintainers to pull my changes into their project.

speaker: ALEX
text: That is exactly it. Review is the feedback process on a PR. A reviewer can leave a comment, approve the change, or request changes before it can be merged.

speaker: JAMIE
text: And good review is not just thumbs up or thumbs down. It should be kind, specific, and useful.

speaker: ALEX
text: Yes. You may also see a draft PR. Draft means the work is visible, but the author is signaling that it is not ready for final review yet.

speaker: JAMIE
text: That is useful in learning settings too. A review-ready draft or a clear contribution plan can be real evidence that someone understands the workflow, even before a maintainer merges anything.

speaker: ALEX
text: Merging is combining changes from one branch into another. GitHub projects may use a merge commit, squash and merge, or rebase and merge, depending on how they want the history to look.

speaker: JAMIE
text: And then there is the famous merge conflict.

speaker: ALEX
text: A merge conflict happens when two branches changed the same part of the same file in incompatible ways. Git pauses because it cannot decide which version should win.

speaker: JAMIE
text: Those conflict markers are the lines with less-than signs, equals signs, and greater-than signs.

speaker: ALEX
text: Yes. You resolve the file by choosing the final content, removing the markers, saving the file, and committing the resolution. It feels intimidating the first time, but it is a normal collaboration moment.

speaker: JAMIE
text: Let's talk about the people words, because GitHub is not just commands.

speaker: ALEX
text: A maintainer is someone with responsibility for a repository, often with write or admin access. A contributor is anyone who helps, whether through code, docs, issues, design, testing, accessibility feedback, or review.

speaker: JAMIE
text: And a collaborator?

speaker: ALEX
text: A collaborator is someone who has been granted access to work directly in a repository, usually more access than a typical outside contributor. Triage is the work of reviewing new issues, adding labels, asking clarifying questions, and routing work to the right place.

speaker: JAMIE
text: Labels are those colored tags, like bug, documentation, good first issue, or accessibility.

speaker: ALEX
text: Right. A milestone groups issues and pull requests around a goal, such as a release or a workshop deadline. GitHub Projects can organize work in boards, tables, and views so a team can track progress.

speaker: JAMIE
text: Community files are part of that collaboration picture too.

speaker: ALEX
text: They are. A README explains what the project is. A LICENSE tells people what they are allowed to do with the code. CONTRIBUTING explains how to help. A code of conduct sets expectations for behavior.

speaker: JAMIE
text: And templates can guide issues and pull requests so people do not start from a blank box.

speaker: ALEX
text: Exactly. You may also see SECURITY for reporting vulnerabilities, SUPPORT for help channels, GitHub Discussions for broader community conversations, a wiki for multi-page documentation, and Gists for small shareable snippets.

speaker: JAMIE
text: What about the quick slang pile?

speaker: ALEX
text: A few common ones: LGTM means looks good to me. WIP means work in progress. CI means continuous integration, where automated checks run on changes. CD can mean continuous delivery or continuous deployment, depending on the project.

speaker: ALEX
text: Now for the Git terms that sound scarier than they usually are. HEAD, in all caps, is Git's pointer to your current branch or commit.

speaker: JAMIE
text: Detached HEAD is the one that makes people wonder if they broke everything.

speaker: ALEX
text: A detached HEAD means you are looking at a specific commit instead of working on a branch. It can happen when you check out an old commit, a tag, or a commit hash directly.

speaker: JAMIE
text: What does that mean for my work?

speaker: ALEX
text: You can look around safely, but new commits made there may be hard to find unless you create a branch. The fix is usually to create a branch at that point with `git switch -c branch-name`, or switch back to an existing branch if you were only inspecting history.

speaker: JAMIE
text: Stash is another useful safety word.

speaker: ALEX
text: Stash temporarily saves uncommitted changes so you can switch tasks or update your branch without committing unfinished work. A common flow is `git stash`, do the other task, then `git stash pop` to bring the changes back.

speaker: JAMIE
text: And if I want to see what I stashed?

speaker: ALEX
text: Use `git stash list`. You can use `git stash apply` to reapply without removing the stash, or `git stash drop` when you are sure you no longer need it.

speaker: JAMIE
text: Rebase is where people get nervous.

speaker: ALEX
text: Rebase replays your commits on top of another branch. Merge preserves the branch history and creates a merge point. Rebase can make history more linear, but it rewrites commit history.

speaker: JAMIE
text: So when is rebase reasonable?

speaker: ALEX
text: It is usually reasonable on your own local branch before you share it, or when your team explicitly uses that workflow. Do not rebase shared branches casually, because rewriting history can disrupt other people's work.

speaker: JAMIE
text: And cherry-pick?

speaker: ALEX
text: Cherry-pick copies one specific commit from one branch onto another. It is useful when you need one fix without bringing over every other change from that branch.

speaker: JAMIE
text: Force push sounds like the red button.

speaker: ALEX
text: It deserves caution. Force push overwrites the remote branch with your local history. It may be needed after a rebase on your own branch, but it is not okay on shared branches unless the team has agreed.

speaker: JAMIE
text: There is a safer version, right?

speaker: ALEX
text: Use `--force-with-lease` instead of plain force push when you can. It checks whether someone else updated the remote branch before overwriting it, which helps prevent accidental damage.

speaker: ALEX
text: A SHA or hash is the unique identifier for a commit or Git object. You will often see a short version, like seven characters, in GitHub links and commit lists.

speaker: JAMIE
text: A tag is a name attached to a specific commit, often for a version.

speaker: ALEX
text: Yes. A release builds on a tag and adds release notes, downloadable files, or other packaged information for users.

speaker: JAMIE
text: Then GitHub Actions is the automation system.

speaker: ALEX
text: Right. An Action runs workflows, and a workflow is an automated process defined in the repository. CI/CD workflows might run tests, check formatting, build documentation, or deploy a site.

speaker: JAMIE
text: And status checks are the pass or fail results that show up on a pull request.

speaker: ALEX
text: Exactly. A status check might say the tests passed, the build failed, or an accessibility check needs attention. Maintainers often require important checks to pass before merging.

speaker: JAMIE
text: What is a webhook?

speaker: ALEX
text: A webhook sends information to another service when something happens on GitHub, like a push, issue comment, or pull request event. It is a way to connect GitHub activity to other tools.

speaker: JAMIE
text: And profile?

speaker: ALEX
text: Your GitHub profile is your public identity on GitHub. It can show your repositories, contributions, bio, links, and sometimes a profile README.

speaker: JAMIE
text: The glossary also needs the accessibility words we keep using in this series.

speaker: ALEX
text: A screen reader is software that reads interface content aloud or sends it to a braille display. NVDA, JAWS, VoiceOver, and TalkBack are common examples.

speaker: JAMIE
text: Landmarks and headings are navigation structure.

speaker: ALEX
text: Yes. Headings organize content by level, like heading level 1 for the page title and heading level 2 for major areas. Landmarks identify regions such as main content, navigation, search, and footer.

speaker: JAMIE
text: ARIA is pronounced AIR-ee-uh, right?

speaker: ALEX
text: Right. ARIA stands for Accessible Rich Internet Applications. It can add accessibility information to custom interface elements, but native HTML should come first whenever it can do the job.

speaker: JAMIE
text: Focus is the current place my keyboard or assistive technology is interacting with.

speaker: ALEX
text: Exactly. Tab order is the path focus follows as you press Tab. A good tab order matches the visual and logical reading order, does not trap people, and makes every interactive control reachable.

speaker: JAMIE
text: So when we review a page, we are not only asking whether it looks good. We are asking whether the structure and keyboard path make sense.

speaker: ALEX
text: Yes, and whether names, roles, labels, error messages, and instructions are available to assistive technology. That is where careful issues and clear reproduction notes really help maintainers.

speaker: ALEX
text: Finally, the agent vocabulary. GitHub Copilot is an AI coding assistant. Depending on the environment, it may suggest code, answer questions, help explain errors, or help draft changes.

speaker: JAMIE
text: And an agent is a little more active than a simple suggestion box.

speaker: ALEX
text: Yes. An agent can follow instructions, use tools, inspect files, and carry out a task within limits. You still review the output, test it, and decide what belongs in the project.

speaker: JAMIE
text: Slash commands are the short commands that start with a slash, like a shortcut in a chat or coding assistant.

speaker: ALEX
text: Right. A prompt is the request you give the tool. An instruction file is a project-level guide that tells the assistant how to behave, such as coding style, testing expectations, accessibility requirements, or documentation tone.

speaker: JAMIE
text: This connects to the later accessibility agent work too.

speaker: ALEX
text: It does. The Accessibility Agents collection is a living catalog, so it grows over time. Challenge 15 is browse-first, and learners do not need to fork that repository just to complete the discovery challenge.

speaker: JAMIE
text: Completing that discovery challenge unlocks the Capstone Project and the structured bonus path, right?

speaker: ALEX
text: Yes. Challenge 16 is titled Capstone Project. It can involve a contribution to Accessibility Agents, GLOW, or another meaningful repository, and review-ready drafts or contribution plans can count as valid evidence of completion.

speaker: JAMIE
text: And Day 1 contributions happen somewhere else.

speaker: ALEX
text: They happen in the Learning Room repository, which is provisioned for each learner. That is where the issue, branch, commit, pull request, and merge workflow is practiced end to end.

speaker: JAMIE
text: Let's end with a quick pronunciation pass for the words people may only have read.

speaker: ALEX
text: Git has a hard G. GitHub is Git-hub. Repo is REE-poh. Org is org. PR is P R. SHA can be shah or S H A.

speaker: JAMIE
text: More please.

speaker: ALEX
text: ARIA is AIR-ee-uh. CI/CD is C I slash C D. YAML is often YAM-ul. `.gitignore` is usually spoken as dot gitignore. `HEAD` is head, even though it is written in capital letters.

speaker: JAMIE
text: And when a term gets fuzzy, do not try to memorize every definition at once.

speaker: ALEX
text: Look it up, read the nearby related terms, and connect it to the workflow you are doing right now. If a fact might have changed, use the official GitHub documentation, release notes, and linked references as the current source of truth.

speaker: JAMIE
text: That makes the glossary less like homework and more like a map you keep beside you.

speaker: ALEX
text: Exactly. The win is not knowing every word before you start. It is being able to recover your place when a new term appears, then keep contributing with confidence.
